en: The Parivāra:
The Analysis of the Monastic Rules (Bhikkhuvibhaṅga), First Part.
1.1 The Chapter on the Formulation of Rules 1.
The Section on Defeat (Pārājika-kaṇḍa) Homage to that Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Self-Awakened One.
Where was this first *pārājika* rule laid down by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, who is an Arhat, a perfectly awakened Buddha—with reference to whom, and on account of what matter?
Is there a primary laying down (*paññatti*) therein, a supplementary laying down (*anupaññatti*), or a laying down for an unarisen offense (*anuppannapaññatti*)?
Is it a universal laying down (*sabbatthapaññatti*) or a partial laying down (*padesapaññatti*)?
Is it a common designation or an uncommon designation?
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
In which of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is it immersed, and in which is it included?
By which summary does it come under summary?
To which of the four failures does it belong?
To which of the seven classes of offenses does it belong?
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
Of the four legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which legal issue is it?
Of the seven principles for settling disputes (*samatha*), by how many principles for settling is it settled?
What therein is the discipline (vinaya)? What therein is the further discipline (abhivinaya)?
What therein is the Pātimokkha? What therein is the higher Pātimokkha (adhipātimokkha)?
What is failure (vipatti)?
What is the attainment?
What is the practice?
For how many reasons did the Blessed One prescribe the first *pārājika* offense?
Who train? Who have trained?
Where is it established?
Who preserves it?
Whose word is it?
By whom was it brought forth?
Where was this first *pārājika* rule laid down by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka.
On what matter? On the matter that Sudinna, the son of Kalandaka, engaged in sexual intercourse with his former wife; it was on this matter.
Is there therein a rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), and a rule for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one rule and two supplementary rules;
there is no rule for what has not yet arisen therein.
Is it a rule of universal application or a rule of limited application?
It is a rule of universal application.
Is it a common rule or an uncommon rule?
A common designation.
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
It is a designation from both sides.
In which of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which is it contained?
It is included in the Introduction (Nidāna) and contained in the Introduction.
By which recitation does it come to be recited?
It comes under the second summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
It is failure in virtue.
Of the seven classes of offenses, which class of offense is it?
It is the class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech.
Among the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which kind of legal issue is it?
The legal issue concerning offenses.
By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes is it settled?
It is settled by two principles for settling disputes.
By means of resolution face-to-face (*sammukhāvinaya*) and by means of acting according to what has been admitted (*paṭiññātakaraṇa*).
What therein is the discipline (*vinaya*), and what therein is the further discipline (*abhivinaya*)?
The formulation (*paññatti*) is the discipline; the analysis (*vibhatti*) is the further discipline.
What therein is the Pātimokkha, and what therein is the Adhipātimokkha?
The formulation (paññatti) is the Pātimokkha; the exposition (vibhatti) is the Adhipātimokkha.
What is failure (vipatti)?
Non-restraint is failure.
What is success?
Restraint is success.
What is the practice?
It is that one undertakes and trains in the rules of training for as long as life lasts, until death, thinking:
"I shall not do such a thing. For how many reasons did the Blessed One prescribe the first *pārājika* offense?
The Blessed One laid down the first *pārājika* rule for ten reasons:
for the well-being of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of individuals who are difficult to manage, for the ease of living of well-behaved bhikkhus,
for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives.
For the inspiration of those without faith, for the increase of those with faith, for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
Who train? Both those in training (sekkhā) and virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) train.
Who are those who have trained in the training?
The Arahants are those who have trained in the training.
Wherein do they stand?
It is established among those who desire training.
Who preserve it?
Those for whom it is appropriate preserve it.
Whose word is it?
It is the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By whom was it brought?
Handed down in succession:
Upāli, Dāsaka,
Soṇaka, and likewise Siggava.
With Moggaliputta as the fifth,
these [monks] [were established] in the land named Jambusiri;
then Mahinda and Itthiya,
Uttiyo, Sambalo likewise,
and the wise one named Bhadda—
these were Nāgas of great wisdom.
Having come here from Jambudīpa,
they recited the Vinaya and the Piṭaka in Tambapaṇṇi.
They recited the five Nikāyas and the seven treatises;
then the wise Ariṭṭha—
And Tissa-datta the wise,
Viśārada Kāḷasumana,
and the elder named Dīgha;
And the wise Dīghasumana;
again, Kāḷasumana,
the Elder Nāga, and Buddharakkhita.
The wise elder Tissa and the learned elder Deva;
and again, the wise Sumanas.
Confident in the Vinaya,
the learned Cūḷanāga is as unassailable as an elephant.
And he named Dhammapālita,
who was highly honored in Rohaṇa;
his disciple was of great wisdom.
Named Khema, a master of the three Piṭakas,
you shone pre-eminently in wisdom like the king of stars upon this island.
Upatissa was wise,
and Phussadeva was a great speaker;
then again, Sumana was wise.
Named Puppha, he was of great learning;
a great speaker and a great sage,
he was skilled in all the Piṭakas.
Furthermore, Upāli was wise,
confident in the Vinaya,
a great nāga, and possessed of great wisdom.
Skilled in the lineage of the true Dhamma,
the wise Abhaya was likewise proficient in all the Piṭakas.
And the wise Elder Tissa was confident in the Vinaya;
his disciple was possessed of great wisdom.
Named Puppha, he was one of great learning;
protecting the Dispensation,
he was established in Jambudīpa.
And the wise Cūḷābhaya,
confident in the Vinaya,
and the wise Elder Tissa.
Cūḷadeva, who was wise and skilled in the lineage of the true Dhamma,
was also confident in the Vinaya.
And the wise Elder Siva,
skilled in all matters of the Vinaya—
these are Nāgas of great wisdom.
Knowing the Vinaya and skilled in the Path,
they proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was this second *pārājika* rule laid down by that Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
Concerning Dhaniya, the potter’s son. On what basis?
On the basis that Dhaniya, the potter’s son, took wood belonging to the king without it being given to him. On that basis.
One is a formal rule (paññatti), one is a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins does it originate?
It originates from three origins.
It may arise from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may arise from both speech and mind, but not from the body;
it may arise from body, speech, and mind... [and so on].
Where was the third *pārājika* laid down?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a number of bhikkhus.
On what basis?
On the basis that a number of bhikkhus took one another’s lives; on that basis.
One is a primary rule (paññatti), one is a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins does it originate?
It originates from three origins.
It may arise from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may arise from both speech and mind, but not from the body;
it may arise from body, speech, and mind... [and so on].
Where was the fourth *pārājika* laid down?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River. On what basis?
On the basis that the monks from the banks of the Vaggumudā River spoke in praise of one another’s superhuman states (uttarimanussadhamma) to householders. On that basis.
One is a primary rule (paññatti), one is a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, from how many origins does it originate?
It originates from three origins.
It may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from the body;
it may originate from body, speech, and mind... [and so on].
The four *pārājika* offenses are concluded.
Its summary verse is:
Sexual intercourse, taking what is not given, and...
Beyond human contact;
the four pārājikas,
the grounds for cutting off, beyond doubt.
2. The Section on Saṅghādisesa Offenses:
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule regarding one who intentionally emits semen formulated by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
With reference to whom was it formulated?
In regard to what matter?
Is there therein a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), or a rule for an unarisen offense (anuppannapaññatti)?
Is it a universal rule (sabbatthapaññatti) or a partial rule (padesapaññatti)?
Is it a common designation or an uncommon designation?
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
In which of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which is it contained?
By which summary does it come under a summary?
To which of the four failures does it belong?
To which of the seven classes of offenses does it belong?
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
Of the four legal issues, which legal issue is it?
Of the seven principles for settling disputes, by how many principles is it settled?
What therein is the discipline (vinaya), what therein is the further discipline (abhivinaya)?
What therein is the Pātimokkha, what therein is the higher Pātimokkha?
What is failure, what is success, and what is the practice?
For how many reasons did the Blessed One prescribe a *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who intentionally emits semen?
Who are those training? Who are those whose training is completed?
Wherein is it established?
Who preserves it?
Whose word is it?
By whom was it brought?
Where was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down by the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—for one who intentionally discharges semen?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Seyyasaka. On what basis?
On the basis that the Venerable Seyyasaka, having made an effort with his hand, discharged semen; on that basis.
Is there therein a rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), and a rule for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one rule and one supplementary rule;
there is no rule for what has not yet arisen therein.
Is it a universal prescription or a partial prescription?
It is a universal prescription.
Is it a common prescription or an uncommon prescription?
Is it an uncommon designation?
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
It is a designation from one side.
In which of the five recitations of the Pātimokkha is it included, and in which is it contained?
It is included in the Introduction (Nidāna) and contained in the Introduction.
By which recitation does it come to be recited?
It comes under the third summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
It is failure in virtue.
Of the seven classes of offenses, which class of offense is it?
It is the *saṅghādisesa* class of offense.
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech.
Among the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which kind of legal issue is it?
The legal issue concerning offenses.
By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes is it settled?
It is settled by two principles for settling disputes.
By means of resolution in the presence of the accused and by means of acting according to what has been admitted.
What therein is the Vinaya, and what therein is the Abhivinaya?
The formal rule (paññatti) is the Vinaya; the detailed analysis (vibhatti) is the Abhivinaya.
What therein is the *pātimokkha*, and what therein is the *adhipātimokkha*?
The formulation (*paññatti*) is the *pātimokkha*; the analysis (*vibhatti*) is the *adhipātimokkha*.
What is failure (*vipatti*)?
Non-restraint is failure.
What is success?
Restraint is success.
What is the practice?
It is training in the rules of training by undertaking them for as long as life lasts, until death, with the thought:
"I shall not do such a thing. For how many reasons did the Blessed One prescribe this Saṅghādisesa offense for one who intentionally discharges semen?
The Blessed One laid down the offense entailing suspension (saṅghādisesa) for one who intentionally emits semen out of eight reasons:
for the welfare of the Saṅgha, for the comfort of the Saṅgha, for the restraint of persons who are difficult to manage, for the ease of well-behaved bhikkhus,
for the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives.
For the inspiration of those without faith, for the increase of those with faith, for the endurance of the true Dhamma, and for the support of the Vinaya.
Who train? Both those in training (sekkhā) and virtuous worldlings (puthujjanakalyāṇaka) train.
Who are those who have trained in the training?
The Arahants are those who have trained in the training.
Wherein do they stand?
It is established among those who desire training.
Who preserves it?
Those for whom it is appropriate preserve it.
Whose word is it?
It is the word of the Blessed One, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One.
By whom was it brought?
Handed down through succession:
Upāli, Dāsaka,
as well as Soṇaka and Siggava.
With Moggaliputta as the fifth,
these [were the teachers] in the land called Jambusiri;
then came Mahinda and Itthiya.
Uttiyo, Sambalo likewise,
and the wise one named Bhadda—
these were Nāgas of great wisdom.
They came here from Jambudīpa;
they taught the Vinaya,
the Piṭaka of Tambapaṇṇi.
They recited the five Nikāyas and the seven treatises;
then the wise Ariṭṭha—
And Tissa-datta the wise,
Visāradakāḷasumana,
and the elder named Dīgha;
And the wise Dīghasumana,
furthermore Kāḷasumana,
the Elder Nāga, and Buddharakkhita.
The wise elder Tissa and the learned elder Deva;
furthermore, the wise Sumana.
Confident in the Vinaya,
the learned Cūḷanāga is like an elephant, difficult to overcome.
And he named Dhammapālita,
who was highly honored in Rohaṇa;
his disciple was one of great wisdom.
Named Khema, a master of the three Piṭakas,
you shone preeminently in wisdom like the king of stars upon this island.
Upatissa was wise,
and Phussadeva was a great speaker;
Sumana, too, was wise.
Named Puppha, he was of great learning;
a great orator and a great sage,
he was skilled in all the Piṭakas.
Furthermore, Upāli was wise,
confident in the Vinaya,
a great nāga of vast intelligence.
Skilled in the lineage of the true Dhamma,
the wise Abhaya was likewise proficient in all the Piṭakas.
And the wise Elder Tissa was confident in the Vinaya;
his disciple was one of great wisdom.
Named Puppha, he was learned in the scriptures;
protecting the teaching,
he was established in Jambudīpa.
And the wise Cūḷābhaya,
confident in the Vinaya;
and the wise Elder Tissa—
Skilled in the lineage of the true Dhamma,
the wise Cūḷadeva was confident in the Vinaya.
And the wise Elder Siva,
skilled in all matters of the Vinaya—
these are Nāgas of great wisdom.
Knowing the Vinaya and skilled in the Path,
they proclaimed the Vinaya Piṭaka on the island of Tambapaṇṇi.
Where was this Saṅghādisesa rule laid down by the Blessed One—the one who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One—concerning one who engages in physical contact with a woman?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Udāyī.
On what account?
On the account of the Venerable Udāyī having engaged in physical contact with a woman; on that account.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech ... [and so on].
Where was the Saṅghādisesa rule concerning one who addresses a woman with lewd words laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī. With reference to whom was it laid down?
Concerning the Venerable Udāyī.
On what matter?
On the matter that the Venerable Udāyī addressed a woman with indecent words; it was on this matter.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins:
it may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech.
It may originate from speech and mind, but not from body;
it may originate from body, speech, and mind... [etc.
Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense formulated for one who speaks in praise of serving one’s own desires in the presence of a woman?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Udāyin.
In what matter?
Venerable Udāyī spoke in praise of serving one's own desires in the presence of a woman; in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins:
it may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from the body.
It may originate from body, speech, and mind … [as before] … Where was the offense entailing suspension for engaging in matchmaking prescribed?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Udāyin.
On what matter?
The Venerable Udāyī engaged in matchmaking; this is the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti) and one supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Regarding the six origins of offenses, it originates through all six origins.
It may originate from the body, not from speech or mind;
it may originate from speech, not from body or mind;
it may originate from both body and speech, not from the mind.
It may originate from both body and mind, but not from speech;
it may originate from both speech and mind, but not from the body;
it may originate from body, speech, and mind …pe….
Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense for one having a hut built by means of begging laid down?
It was laid down at Āḷavī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the monks at Āḷavaka.
On what matter? On the matter that the monks at Āḷavaka had small huts built by means of solicitation. On that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses by means of the six origins ... [etc.
... Where was the Saṅghādisesa offense for one having a large monastery built laid down?
It was laid down at Kosambī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Channa.
In what matter?
Venerable Channa, while clearing a site for a dwelling, had a certain sacred tree cut down; it was in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from six origins ... [as above] ...
Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense for one who groundlessly accuses a bhikkhu of an offense entailing defeat (*pārājika*) laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom? With reference to the monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka.
On account of what matter?
The monks Mettiya and Bhūmajaka groundlessly accused the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta of an offense entailing expulsion (pārājika) on that account.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [and so forth].
Where was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed for one who, taking some part or mere pretext of a legal issue belonging to another category, accuses a bhikkhu of an offense entailing defeat?
It was prescribed at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom was it prescribed?
Concerning the monks from Mettiya and Bhūmajaka. On what basis?
On the basis of this matter:
the monks from Mettiya and Bhūmajaka, taking some part and a mere pretext of an unrelated legal issue, accused the Venerable Dabba Mallaputta of an offense entailing expulsion; it was on that basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

It originates from three of the six origins of offenses (āpatti-samuṭṭhāna) … [as above] … Where was the Saṅghādisesa offense prescribed for a monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha and does not desist after being admonished up to the third time?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
With reference to Devadatta.
In regard to what matter?
Devadatta strove for the schism of the harmonious Saṅgha; it was in regard to that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—
it originates from body, speech, and mind.
…pe… Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense prescribed for those monks who follow a schism and do not desist even after being admonished up to three times?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhus.
In regard to what matter?
There were many bhikkhus who became followers and partisans of Devadatta as he was striving to cause a schism in the Saṅgha; it was on that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from body, speech, and mind.
… [as above] … Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense prescribed for a monk who is difficult to speak with and does not desist even after being admonished up to three times?
It was laid down at Kosambī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Channa.
In what matter?
The Venerable Channa, when being addressed by the monks in accordance with the Dhamma, made himself one who should not be spoken to; in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from body, speech, and mind.
…pe… Where was the *saṅghādisesa* offense for a monk who is a corrupter of families, not relinquishing [his conduct] despite being pressed up to the third time, laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the monks Assaji and Punabbasuka.

In what matter? The monks Assaji and Punabbasuka, having had a formal act of banishment (*pabbājanīya-kamma*) carried out against them by the Saṅgha, brought [the Saṅgha] to states of favoritism, ill-will, delusion, and fear; it was in that matter.
There is one rule (*paññatti*).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from body, speech, and mind.
… [as above] … The thirteen *saṅghādisesa* rules are finished.
Its summary verse:
Relinquishing, bodily contact,
lewdness, and self-indulgence;
Matchmaking, a hut,
and a monastery; groundless [accusation],
something trifling, and causing a schism.
And those who follow after him;
the difficult-to-correct and the corrupter of families—
these are the thirteen Saṅghādisesa offenses.
3. The Section on the Indeterminate (Aniyata-kanda).
Where was the first indeterminate offense prescribed by that Blessed One—who knows and sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One? With reference to whom was it laid down?
In what matter?

Therein there are: a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), a rule for an unarisen offense (anuppannapaññatti), a universal rule (sabbatthapaññatti), a partial rule (padesapaññatti), a common rule (sādhāraṇapaññatti), an uncommon rule (asādhāraṇapaññatti), a rule for one side (ekatopaññatti), a rule for both sides (ubhatopaññatti), and the five recitations of the Pātimokkha.
In what is it included? To which category does it belong? Under which summary does it come? To which of the four failures does it belong?
To which of the seven classes of offenses does it belong? By how many origins does it originate among the six origins of offenses? To which of the four legal issues does it belong? Of the seven...
By how many means of settling (*samatha*) are disputes settled? What therein is the discipline (*vinaya*)? What therein is the further discipline (*abhivinaya*)?
What therein is the Pātimokkha? What therein is the higher Pātimokkha? What is failure (*vipatti*)? What is success (*sampatti*)? What is practice (*paṭipatti*)?
For how many reasons did the Blessed One prescribe the first undetermined rule (*aniyata*)? Who train [in it]? Who have completed their training?
Where was it established, who preserved it, whose word is it, and by whom was it brought forth?
Where was the first undetermined offense (aniyata) laid down by that Blessed One—the one who knows, the one who sees, the Worthy One, the Perfectly Enlightened One?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Udāyin.
On account of what matter?
The Venerable Udāyī sat down alone with a woman on a secluded, concealed seat suitable for sexual intercourse; this was the case.
Is there therein a formal rule (paññatti), a supplementary rule (anupaññatti), or a rule for an unarisen offense (anuppannapaññatti)?
There is one formal rule.
There is no subsequent rule (anupaññatti) nor a rule for what has not yet arisen (anuppannapaññatti) in that case.
Is it a universal rule (sabbatthapaññatti) or a partial rule (padesapaññatti)?
It is a universal rule.
Is it a common designation or an uncommon designation?
It is an uncommon designation.
Is it a designation from one side or a designation from both sides?
A single designation.
In what is the recitation of the five Pātimokkhas subsumed, and in what are they included?
They are subsumed in the Nidāna and included in the Nidāna.
By which summary does it come under a summary?
It comes under the fourth summary.
Of the four failures, which failure is it?
It may be a failure in virtue; it may be a failure in conduct.
Among the seven classes of offenses, to which class of offense does it belong?

It may be a class of offenses involving defeat (pārājika), it may be a class of offenses involving formal meeting of the Saṅgha (saṅghādisesa), or it may be a class of offenses requiring expiation (pācittiya).
Of the six origins of offenses, by how many origins does it originate?
It originates by one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech.
Of the four kinds of legal issues (*adhikaraṇa*), which one is it?
It is a legal issue arising from an offense (*āpattādhikaraṇa*).
By how many of the seven principles for settling disputes (*samatha*) is it settled?

With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of six monks.
In what matter?
In the matter that the group of six monks, having stayed [overnight] repeatedly, ate alms-food from a public rest-house. In that matter.
One is a primary rule (paññatti), one is a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins in the case of wool... [etc.
...Where was the offense of expiation for eating in a group laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
With reference to Devadatta.
In what matter? Devadatta, together with his retinue, ate after repeatedly soliciting from families; it was in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti) and seven supplementary rules (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: [the offense regarding] wool... [etc.
... Where was the *pācittiya* for eating in succession laid down?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhus.
In regard to what matter?
A number of bhikkhus, having been invited elsewhere, ate elsewhere; this was the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti) and four supplementary rules (anupaññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: [the offense] regarding the kaṭhina robe... [etc.]... [originates from] both.
"Having accepted two or three bowlfuls of cakes, for one who accepts more than that, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?"
Concerning a number of bhikkhus.
On what matter?
On the matter of a number of bhikkhus receiving without moderation; on that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
It originates from six origins of offenses; it originates by way of six origins. ... [etc. ...
For one who, having finished eating and refused further food, eats fresh or cooked food that is not left over, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhus.
In what matter? In this matter:
several bhikkhus, having already finished their meal and being invited to stop, ate again elsewhere.
In that matter, there is one formal rule (paññatti) and one supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins in the case of the *kathina* robe... [etc. ...

For one who, when a monk has already finished his meal and refused further food, invites him to accept fresh or soft food that is not left over, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a certain bhikkhu.
On account of what matter?
A certain bhikkhu invited another bhikkhu who had already finished his meal and refused further food to accept a gift of fresh, non-leftover food; this was the basis for the offense.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Among the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [and so on] …
For one who eats solid food or soft food at the wrong time, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of seventeen bhikkhus.
On what matter?
On the matter that the group of seventeen bhikkhus ate food at the wrong time. On that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: [the offense regarding] wool... pe ...
For one who eats fresh or cooked food that has been stored, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom? With reference to the Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa.
In what matter?
The Venerable Belaṭṭhasīsa ate food that had been stored; it was in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins in the case of wool for rugs (*eḷakaloma*) … [as before] … Where was the offense of expiation (*pācittiya*) prescribed for one who, having requested delicacies for oneself, eats them?
It was prescribed at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
On account of what matter?
The group of six monks requested delicacies for their own sake and ate them; this was the basis for the rule.
There is one formal enactment (paññatti) and one subsequent enactment (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from four origins … [and so on] …
For one who takes food that has not been given through the gateway of the mouth, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a certain bhikkhu.
With reference to what matter?
Concerning the matter that a certain bhikkhu took food into his mouth that had not been given to him. That is the matter.
One rule, one addition to the rule.
It originates from two of the six origins of offenses regarding wool... [etc.
...The fourth section on food is concluded.
5.5. The Chapter on the Naked Ascetics (Acelakavagga).

For one who gives hard food or soft food with his own hand to a naked ascetic (acelaka), or to a male wanderer (paribbājaka), or to a female wanderer (paribbājikā), there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Where was it prescribed? It was prescribed at Vesālī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Ānanda.
On account of what matter?
The Venerable Ānanda, thinking one wandering female ascetic was two, gave her two cakes; this is the case.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: as in the case of wool... [and so on].

For one who dismisses a bhikkhu by saying, "Come, friend, let us enter a village or a town for alms," whether having caused him to be given [alms] or not having caused him to be given [alms], there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī. With reference to whom?
With reference to Upananda the Sakyan.
Concerning the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son. On what basis?

On the basis that the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son said to a bhikkhu, "Come, friend, let us enter the village for alms," and then dismissed him without having had anything given to him. It was on this basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as above] … For one who intrudes upon a family where food is being consumed and takes a seat, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan.
In what matter?
In the matter where the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son intruded himself and sat down in a family engaged in a meal;
in that matter there is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech ... [as above] ...
For one who sits down in private on a concealed seat with a woman, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan.
In what matter?
The Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta sat down in private on a secluded seat together with a woman; it was in this matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech ... [etc. ...
For one who sits in private alone with a woman, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan.
In what matter? In this matter:
the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son sat alone with a woman in private; in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, not from speech ... [as above] ...

It is an offense entailing expiation for a monk who, having been invited with a meal, goes on a visit to families before or after the meal without having informed a monk who is present. Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan.
In what matter?
The Venerable Upananda the Sakyaputta, having been invited for a meal together with his companions, went on a visit to families before the meal and after the meal; it was in this matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti) and four supplementary rules (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins regarding the *kathina* cloth... [etc.
...What is the offense of expiation for requesting medicinal requisites beyond that limit?
It was laid down among the Sakyans.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
On account of what matter?
The group of six monks did not wait when they were told by Mahānāma the Sakyan, “Venerable sirs, please wait until tomorrow,” in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates through all six origins … [and so on].
For one who goes to see an army on active service, it is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of six monks.
In regard to what matter?
It was on this matter that the group of six monks went to see an army on active service.
One is a formal rule (paññatti), one is a supplementary rule (anupaññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins in the case of wool... [etc.
... Where was the offense of expiation for staying with an army for more than three nights laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six bhikkhus.
In what matter?
In the matter of the group of six monks staying with an army for more than three nights; in that matter, there is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins in the case of *eḷakaloma*... [etc. ...
For one who goes to a battle, there is an offense of expiation (*pācittiya*). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
In regard to what matter?
The group of six monks went to a military parade; this is the basis for the offense.
There is one rule.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: [as in the case of] wool... etc.
The fifth chapter, on the Naked Ascetics, is concluded.
5.6. The Chapter on Drinking Liquor:
Regarding the offense of expiation for drinking fermented or distilled liquors—where was it prescribed?
It was laid down at Kosambī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the Venerable Sāgata.
In what matter?
In the matter of the Venerable Sāgata drinking liquor;
in that matter there is one rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins:
it may originate from the body, not from speech or mind;
or it may originate from both the body and the mind, not from speech ... [and so on].
Regarding the offense of expiation for tickling with the fingers: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of six bhikkhus. On what basis?
On the basis that the group of six bhikkhus made a bhikkhu laugh by tickling him with their fingers. That is the basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech ... [and so on].
Regarding the offense of expiation for laughing in water: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the group of seventeen bhikkhus.
On what basis?
On the basis of the group of seventeen bhikkhus playing in the water of the Aciravatī River.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from both body and mind, but not from speech ... [and so on].
Regarding the offense of expiation for disrespect: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Kosambī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Channa.
On account of what matter?
On account of the matter that the Venerable Channa showed disrespect.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as above] … Where was the offense of expiation (pācittiya) for frightening a bhikkhu laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
In what matter?
In the matter of the group of six bhikkhus frightening a bhikkhu; in that matter, there is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins ... [as before] ...
For one who, having kindled a fire, warms himself, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down among the Bhaggas.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhus.
In regard to what matter?
A number of bhikkhus kindled a fire and warmed themselves; this was the basis for the rule.
There is one primary rule (paññatti) and two subsequent rules (anupaññatti).
Regarding the six origins of offenses, it originates through all six origins … [as detailed].
"For one who bathes every half-month, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
"It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?"
Concerning a number of bhikkhus.
On what basis?
On the basis that a number of bhikkhus, even after seeing the king, bathed without knowing moderation. On that basis.
There is one original rule (paññatti) and six supplementary rules (anupaññatti).
Is it a universal rule (sabbatthapaññatti) or a partial rule (padesapaññatti)?
It is a partial rule.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins in the case of the wool of rams ... [as above] ...
Regarding the offense of expiation for one who uses a new robe without having applied any one of the three methods of disfiguring it: where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a number of bhikkhus.
In regard to what matter?
A number of bhikkhus did not recognize their own robes; this is the case in that instance.
There is one rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: ... [as in the case of] wool for rugs ... pe ... .

For a bhikkhu, a bhikkhunī, a female trainee, a male novice, or a female novice who, having personally assigned a robe to another, uses it without having had the assignment rescinded, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya).
Where was this laid down? It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son. On account of what matter?
On account of this matter:
the Venerable Upananda the Sakyan son, having himself assigned a robe to a bhikkhu, used it without having formally relinquished his own claim to it. It was on account of this matter.
There is one rule.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins: [it concerns] the kaṭhina cloth ... pe ...
For a monk who misplaces his bowl, or his robe, or his sitting mat, or his needle case, or his waistband, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
In what matter?
In the matter of the group of six monks misappropriating both the alms-bowls and the robes of other monks.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as above] … The sixth section:
On Intoxicants (Surāmerayavagga). 5.7.
The section on Living Beings (Sappāṇakavagga).
For one who intentionally deprives a living being of life, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning the Venerable Udāyī.
On account of what matter?
On account of the matter that the Venerable Udāyī intentionally deprived a living being of life. On account of that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as above] … For one who knowingly consumes water containing living beings, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
In what matter?
In that matter wherein the group of six monks knowingly consumed water containing living beings;
in that matter there is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [as above] … For one who reopens a legal issue that has been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, knowing it to be so, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
On account of what matter?
The group of six monks, knowing that a legal issue had been settled in accordance with the Dhamma, reopened it for a formal act regarding that same matter.
There is one rule.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins … [and so on] … *Note: This passage refers to the Saṅghādisesa offense (No. 10) concerning reopening a settled legal issue.*
For a bhikkhu who knowingly conceals a grave offense, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a certain bhikkhu.
On what basis?
On the basis that a certain bhikkhu knowingly concealed a grave offense of another bhikkhu; it was on this basis.
There is one classification.
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin—it originates from body, speech, and mind. …pe…
For one who ordains a person knowing them to be less than twenty years of age, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Rājagaha.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a number of bhikkhus.
On what matter?
On the matter that a number of bhikkhus knowingly conferred the full admission on a person less than twenty years of age. On that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from three origins ... [etc. ...
For one who knowingly makes an appointment with a caravan of thieves and sets out on a journey along the same road, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was this rule laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to a certain bhikkhu.
In what matter?
A certain bhikkhu, knowing [he was with] a band of thieves, made an appointment and set out on the same road with them; in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from two origins:
it may originate from body and mind, but not from speech;
or it may originate from body, speech, and mind …pe….
For one who sets out on a journey along a highway in company with a woman, there is an offense of expiation (pācittiya). Where was it laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
Concerning a certain bhikkhu. On what basis?
On the basis of a certain bhikkhu who, having made an appointment with a woman, set out on a journey along a highway; it was on that basis.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from four origins … [as above] … For one who does not relinquish an evil view after being pressed up to the third time, there is an offense entailing confession (pācittiya). Where was this laid down?
It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom? With reference to the bhikkhu Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-killer.
In what matter?
In the matter of the monk Ariṭṭha, formerly a vulture-keeper, who did not relinquish an evil view despite being pressed up to the third time; in that matter.
One formal rule (paññatti).
Of the six origins of offenses, it originates from one origin:
it originates from body, speech, and mind. ... [etc. ...

It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six bhikkhus.
In what matter?

The group-of-six monks, knowing that the monk Ariṭṭha was speaking in such a way, had not made amends according to the Dhamma, and had not relinquished that view, ate together with him—in that matter.
There is one formal rule (paññatti).

It was laid down at Sāvatthī.
With reference to whom?
With reference to the group of six monks.
